newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala guerrillas spread soccer-game propaganda.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala guerrillas spread soccer-game propaganda.

text.p: An urban front of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) interrupted a local soccer game near the capital on Sunday to say the rebels were renouncing violence and forming a political party.
The URNG and the government are two weeks away from signing a definitive peace treaty to end 36 years of civil war in which an estimated 140,000 Guatemalans have died or been "disappeared."

As the sun set on the working-class housing development of Joya de la Comunidad just west of the capital, 25 young men and women, their faces covered with blue "URNG" bandannas, took up formation at the edge of a dusty soccer field.
The players begged for time to finish their game, and the guerrillas agreed to wait for 15 minutes and hand out flyers.
People watching the game began to drift toward the guerrillas, starting one-one-one conversations. One elderly woman told a rebel her water bills had doubled.
Everyone laughed when a local drunk tried to panhandle a guerrilla. A stray soccer ball bounced off a television camera.

The guerrillas tried to work fast. Membership in the URNG is still illegal in Guatemala, but the guerrillas will become legitimate citizens and will be allowed to form a political party after peace accords are put into effect on Dec. 29.
After the game, about 150 people, most of them sympathetic, gathered to hear the URNG statement.

"We will never lose our political objective. The change in society involves everyone," the column's leader, "Sgt. Oscar," said as he explained that the URNG's ideological battle was not finished, even if the armed struggle was over.
Some people, young and old, raised their fists in the air and joined chants of "Viva la URNG!"
One young couple listening said they were pleased the URNG would form a party.
"That would be good, because the URNG has always been with the people. They have never harmed anyone," said Oscar Enriquez, who listened with his wife and young child.
In March, the URNG declared a unilateral ceasefire and stopped blowing up bridges and collecting war taxes from busloads of peasants and wealthy farmers.

But urban and rural fronts of the URNG continued to carry out armed propaganda actions until October, when they ceased the campaigns as a conciliatory gesture to the government during a brief crisis in the peace talks.
A week ago the guerrillas resumed surprise, nightly propaganda actions around the capital, usually in poor neighbourhoods and squatters' camps.
